The findings presented in this article are part of a wider ethnographic study aimed at gaining a thick comprehension (Brewer, 2000) of children's consumer behaviour in fashion retail settings (Ironico, 2010). Field research began in 2006 involving the participation in international children's wear exhibitions such as Pitti Immagine Bimbo; in‐depth interviews of marketing, communication and retail professionals; qualitative content analyses of children's wear companies promotional materials (press kits, advertisements, web sites) and long term in‐store observations.
As is well documented in the literature (Bailey, 1982; McNeal, 1998), non‐intrusive observational methods are ideally suited for investigating children behaviour, considering children's limited introspective and verbal skills. In‐store observational studies, in particular, have been previously conducted for investigating parent‐child interactions (Atkin, 1978; Barnard et al., 1977; Darian, 1998; Gaumer and Arnone, 2010; Ishida, 1980; Montemayor and Flannery, 1989; Peters and Stewart, 1981; Pettersson et al., 2004; Rust, 1993; Warren, 2001), children's and adolescents' interactions with peers (Chin, 2001; Montemayor and Flannery, 1989; Russell and Tyler, 2005), children's influence on parents' purchase decisions (Atkin, 1978; Axia, 1996; Gram, 2010; Ishida, 1980; Nørgaard et al., 2007; O'Dougherty et al., 2006), parental mediation of children's consumption (Warren, 2001), children's interaction with the retail environment (Chin, 2001; Langer, 2004; Russell and Tyler, 2005; Rust, 1993), children's purchase behaviour (Brée, 1987; Coughlin and Wong, 2003). However, the use of observational methods for investigating children consumer behaviour is still limited as compared to research designs involving surveys, experiments and personal interviews (Gram, 2010; Mangleburg, 1990).
The observational field study from which this article draws was carried out in ten children's wear stores in Milan: a department store, a variety store, a flagship store, a multibrand store and six retail chains. After collecting general information on the retailers' positioning and patronage through qualitative interviews with the sales personnel, the author carried out a qualitative content analysis of the in‐store environment, visual merchandising techniques and communication activities in order to classify the retail stimuli children were exposed to. Children's lived experience of the retail spaces was then investigated following a child‐centric approach (Banister and Booth, 2005), observing children's interactions with both social (companions, sales personnel, other consumers shopping in the stores) and environmental influences (fixtures, furniture, display units, products, and promotional materials).
Inside each store, six Italian white children – three boys and three girls – were unobtrusively observed, giving a total of 60 subjects. The sample was also subdivided in three subsamples – each one made up of ten boys and ten girls – corresponding to the estimated age groups of 2‐4, 5‐7 and 8‐10 year olds. Each observation began the moment that a child with the features required by the sample frame entered the store and lasted for all his or her shopping experience (approximately 45 minutes). Subsequently, parents or the other adult accompanying persons were informed about the study and were asked for consent to use the gathered information for research purposes.
The observations were conducted by the writer with the aid of a small notepad and a voice recorder. In order not to interfere with the observed subjects' spontaneous behaviours and to minimize their reactivity (Bailey, 1982), interactions of any kind with both children and their companions were avoided and the researcher just browsed as any other customer would. Consequently, field notes were limited to only a few keywords able to render the main facets of the behaviours under investigation. Other more detailed notes were transcribed immediately after informing the subjects about the study. Fieldnotes were extensively copied down in a fieldwork journal and integrated with the audio‐recordings transcripts in the subsequent 24 hours.
The observed events' dynamics was reconstructed focusing on children's lived experiences of the selling space and their relationship with both environmental and social influences. Behaviours were analytically described, giving consideration to the gestural expressiveness, the proxemics and all the other non‐verbal communication aspects. According to an ethnographic approach (Brewer, 2000), all the researcher's sensations, feelings, impressions and emotions experienced during the observations were reported in the fieldwork journal, disclosing all the subjective facets of the interpretation. Afterwards, the ethnographic journal was enriched with the early interpretative hypothesis emerged during both the observations and the recalling of the observed events. In order to identify other possible biases in the researcher's interpretation, the store's owners and sales personnel were periodically in‐depth interviewed.
Field notes were analyzed according to grounded theory (Glaser and Strauss, 1967; Strauss and Corbin, 1990), employing an iterative process of literature review and data collection and analysis (Goulding, 1998; Pettigrew, 2000). The constant comparative method (Glaser and Strauss, 1967; Hammersley, 1989) was employed for generating theoretical categories able to give insights into the symbolic meanings of children's lived experience of the commercial spaces. The properties and dimensions of these categories were then identified until saturation (Pettigrew, 2000). Categories, property and dimensions were finally compared with theoretical propositions, fleshing out a thick interpretation and description of children's in store behaviour.

title: Brigadier Lorimer
resource:
Brigadier Lorimer has been out, he's done his reconnaissance, he's now put in to the planning process, what it is he needs. He will be given what he needs
 


Lord Drayson, Defence Minister








Return to Politics Show homepage here...



British troops in Iraq will not leave the country when they over control of security in the remaining provinces to Iraqi forces, the Defence Minister Lord Drayson told the BBC's Politics Show on Sunday. 

But Lord Drayson also confirmed that troops would not be used to help out US forces - and asked whether if they had spare capacity they could support US troops in Baghdad, he said they "will only stay in Iraq when they have a real job to do."



He confirmed that all requests received through the chain of command had been fulfilled, and that General Lorimer, who will take over in Afghanistan in the spring, would also be given what he needs: "Yes, Brigadier Lorimer has been out, he's done his reconnaissance, he's now put in to the planning process, what it is he needs. He will be given what he needs."

INTERVIEW WITH: LORD DRAYSON, DEFENCE MINISTER




JON SOPEL: I'm joined now by Lord Drayson, the Minister for Defence procurement and welcome to the Politics Show, Lord Drayson.



LORD DRAYSON: Good morning.



JON SOPEL: Tony Blair's promise there, whatever package they want we will do, which seems absolutely unequivocal, then in the Commons this week he said, of course we will listen carefully to any requests that are made to us, that didn't sound quite as clear. 



LORD DRAYSON: Well I think it is clear. He has said, and I have said that whatever the chain of command say that they need to do the tough job that we asked them to do, we will provide it.



JON SOPEL: No if's, buts does matter how much it costs.



LORD DRAYSON: No ifs buts. This is really important. We are undertaking two very difficult operations in Afghanistan and Iraq. We need to make sure that our troops, taking on this very difficult job have all the kit that they need to do the job properly. What's important is what the chain of command say that they need and everything that the chain of command have said that they needed so far, they have got.



JON SOPEL: So why do we still hear so many murmurs of discontent.



LORD DRAYSON: Well I think it's, it's important to recognise that people have different opinions about what is needed to do particular jobs and this is something which I take very seriously. 

I as Afghanistan just last month, talking to the troops, the Parachute Regiment that have, were just coming back and the Royal Marines that were just going over and listening to the troops on the ground, to see what they think of the kit, important point is though is that we do have a military planning process that determines what is needed on an operation and we listened to that planning process and act upon it.



JON SOPEL: But what about, for example Sergeant Steven Brown, of the Royal Marines, in Iraq this week, countless times we have put in requests for what we need extra and it has not arrived.



LORD DRAYSON: It's not correct. Everything that the chain of command have asked for, they have got. 



JON SOPEL: Everything come what may. It's just when you get soldiers, very unusually, making public their concerns, people tend, the public I think, probably tend to believe the soldiers maybe more than they do ministers or the top brass.



LORD DRAYSON: Well it's right that we listen to the soldiers and it's right that ministers like me, talk to and listen to the soldiers, but it's not right for Ministers to infer in how equipment is allocated. I'm sure that Brigadier Gerry Thomas, wouldn't appreciate me interfering in the way in which, and he operates the operation, micromanaging the way in which equipment is allocated. 



JON SOPEL: And in terms of, I mean for example, let's take helicopters. We heard there in that report, Tobias Elwood saying that General Fraser has been asking for more of them. I mean do you simply have more of them to give. 



LORD DRAYSON: Well remember General Fraser is a Canadian Brigadier, he's not a British officer.



JON SOPEL: But answering to the British chain of command.



LORD DRAYSON: This is a NATO operation and as we have heard, there have been many discussions within NATO as to which countries are providing which equipment and there will be a meeting next week to discuss this again. 

But in terms of helicopters, earlier in the summer our commander, Brigadier Ed Butler said that he needed more helicopters, we provided more helicopters. We sent out two Chinooks, we increased the helicopter hours and where we stand now, having spoken to Gerry Thomas, who is the current commander, he says he has the helicopters he needs right now. 



JON SOPEL: I mean what about Brigadier John Lorimer who's going to take over in Afghanistan in the Spring. He's been asking for lots of things. Will he get what he wants.

 

LORD DRAYSON: Yes, Brigadier Lorimer has been out, he's done his reconnaissance, he's now put in to the planning process, what it is he needs. He will be given what he needs. 



JON SOPEL: So that's a hard promise because we spoke to the Ministry of Defence, they say his recommendations are being considered. They didn't, you could have easily come back to us when we made this specific enquiry, and said, he will get what he wants. You said no. His recommendations are being considered.



LORD DRAYSON: Well I'm being very direct with you Jon. It's a, there's a military planning process. The planning process determines what is needed to do the job, that goes through the Ministry of Defence processes, but in the end, there is a determination, by the military of what they need. It is my job, as the Minister of Defence procurement, to make sure they get it. 



JON SOPEL: Okay, let's turn to Iraq now because we've got a detailed timetable or as near as we've got to a detailed timetable for handing over control to Iraqi forces. Does that mean that when we do that we go.



LORD DRAYSON: No. We need to, bear in mind that we're going through a process of handover. We've seen real progress in a number of provinces already being handed over and what that means is rather than British troops doing the patrolling, it's the Iraqi forces, the police and the army doing the patrolling with our troops as a backup in support. 

So our troops are still in theatre, but they're largely in their barracks in that particular region, rather than doing the patrolling. Now we hope that Basra will be successful through operation Sinbad which is taking place now, where we've really learnt some important lessons about how to do this well. If Sinbad goes well, then we hope, it depends on conditions, but we hope in the Spring we will be able to hand over to the Iraq forces, but we will still need our troops to provide what we call operational over-arch.



JON SOPEL: It's very difficult though. I mean I remember at the start of the Iraq war being out there, and the problem was it's very difficult to keep thousands of people in the desert or in barracks, doing nothing. Is that what is being proposed.

 

LORD DRAYSON: No, they're not doing nothing, they're very busy doing training. We've trained hundreds of thousands of the Iraqi security forces, the army and the police and there's a very important job - and when I speak to our troops in Iraq, they tell me how they do and appreciate the job of mentoring and teaching the Iraqi forces. 

There's then a final stage, what we call strategic overwatch, where we are able to leave Iraq, because the Iraqi forces have the competence to be able to take over responsibility. So, really, it's not a direct correlation between being able to do the hand over and troops being able to come home. 



JON SOPEL: Might they be also I don't know, a reserve force for the Americans, if they need, I don't know, a hole plugged in Baghdad or something like that.



LORD DRAYSON: No, I don't think we're getting in to discussing things like that. We have a clear strategy. We have a responsibility for certain areas, certain provinces. We've handed over two already. We expect to be able to hand over a third round about Christmas. We hope that the conditions will be such in the Spring to hand over Basra. We'll have to see. 



JON SOPEL: Could you rule that for example, that if you had, I don't know, all this spare capacity of people sitting in their barracks as you described, that if the Americans needed some help in Baghdad that we might send a couple of thousand troops¿



LORD DRAYSON: There would never be a question of having spare capacity. We are under pressure in terms of the operations which we have to cope with. Our troops will only stay in Iraq when they have a real job to do. Now that job could be patrolling in certain areas, as they are at the moment or...



JON SOPEL: I'm just trying to - sorry to interrupt you, I'm just trying to reconcile you - that with what you said earlier which is that they will largely be in barracks and they will there as a backup force. If they are there as a back-up force, couldn't they possibly be in some circumstances, a back up force to the Americans in some of the hotter places. 



LORD DRAYSON: No, no, they couldn't be in two places at once. So no.



JON SOPEL: Right. So they stay there and then can you give, if everything went to plan in terms of the handover and what you think is the period needed to settle in the Iraqi forces, when it may be that the British troops are home.



LORD DRAYSON: Yes, is depends upon conditions on the ground. We want to bring our troops home as soon as we can, but we are there to help Iraq make the progress which its people, having elected a democratic government, want to see the country go in to that direction. Our troops will come home when the conditions on the ground allow the security to be stable, being run, operated by the Iraqi forces themselves. 



JON SOPEL: A year, two years, five years.



LORD DRAYSON: It depends on the conditions. 



JON SOPEL: Well I'm just saying, if everything went well.



LORD DRAYSON: Well I don't think it's wise for us, for someone like me to get in to predicting what we've said consistency. We have a clear strategy. It's about handing over to the Iraqi forces, so that's about building up their capability. We've seen already, in Al Mutana the way in which the forces were able to cope with...



JON SOPEL: Okay. Let's just talk about Trident which we know came before cabinet this week. Unanimously backing the idea of retaining our independent nuclear deterrent. What are the options. 



LORD DRAYSON: Jon, the cabinet have not made a decision about Trident. There was a presentation to cabinet about the strategic context for defence in the future. There's been no decision. The situation we're in at the moment is there is a White Paper being prepared. That looks at all of the options for the replacement of the deterrent and it is expected that that will be published before the end of the year. 



JON SOPEL: And the choices.



LORD DRAYSON: Well, the, the choices range from maintaining the deterrent on its existing basis, in other words, a submarine base. Or looking at other options such as extending the life of the current system, through to an air base system or a ground base system. Looking at all the different options for the deterrent including the way it could be deployed. 



JON SOPEL: And there's going to be a consultation exercise. What is the point of that. Isn't it for you to decide. You're the experts on this. You should know what's best. I mean you're not going to listen Labour Party members saying, well actually, we would prefer a ground based system are you.



LORD DRAYSON: Well it is right for Ministers to review the issue. There will be a Cabinet discussion and the cabinet will come to a conclusion and it is right that that should take place. But this is going to be a much more open process than similar decisions have been in the past, so there will be the publication of the White Paper and then there will be a full debate.



JON SOPEL: But surely, you're not going to have a defence policy decided either by Labour party members or, I mean, surely you've got to come forward with a clear recommendation - and that will be your assessment.



LORD DRAYSON: Ministers will come forward, after the cabinet have discussed it and come to a conclusion and that conclusion will be made clear. You're right.



JON SOPEL: Okay, Lord Drayson, thank you very much for being with us here on the The Politics Show.

title: 6.2.2 The break-even (BE) curve
resource:
The mark-up and number of firms are related in another way, summarized by the BE curve. When a sector is marked by increasing returns to scale, there is room for only a certain number of firms in a market of a given size. Intuitively, more firms will be able to  survive  if  the  price  is  far  above marginal  cost,  that  is,  if  the  mark-up  is  high.  The  curve  that  captures  this  relationship  is  called  the ‘break-even curve’, or zero-profit curve (BE curve, for short) in Figure 6.3. It has  a  positive  slope  since more firms can break even when the mark-up is high. That is to say, taking the mark-up as given, the BE curve shows the number of firms that can earn enough to cover their fixed cost, say, the cost of setting up a factory.
To  recap,  the  COMP  slopes  downwards  since  more  firms  means  more  competition  and  more competition forces down the mark-up. The BE curve slopes upwards since when there are more firms in the market, each sells less and thus they would need a higher mark-up to cover their costs  (that  is  to say, break even).

It is important to note that firms are not always on the BE curve since they can earn above-normal or below-normal profits for a while.  In  the  long  run,  however,  firms  can  enter  or  exit  the  market,  so  the number of firms rises or falls until the typical firm earns just enough to cover its fixed cost. By contrast, firms are always on the COMP curve since firms can change prices quickly in response to any change in the number of competing firms.
With this in mind, we are ready to work out the equilibrium mark-up, number of firms, price and firm size in a closed economy using Figure 6.4. The right-hand panel combines the BE curve with the COMP curve. The intersection of the two defines the equilibrium mark-up and long-run number of firms. More specifically, the COMP curve tells us that firms would charge a mark-up of μ′ when there are n′ firms in the  market,  and  the  BE curve  tells  us  that  n′  firms  could  break  even  when  the  mark-up  is  μ′.  The equilibrium price is – by definition of the mark-up – just the equilibrium mark-up plus the marginal cost, which  is  shown  by  the  curve  MC. Using  the  MC curve  from  the  left-hand  panel,  we  see  that  the equilibrium price is p′ (this equals μ′ plus MC). The middle panel shows the demand curve, which allows us to see that the total level of consumption implied by the equilibrium price is C′.
The left-hand panel helps us to find the equilibrium firm size, that is, sales per firm, which we denote as x′. This sub-diagram (the left most panel) shows the average and marginal cost curves of a typical firm. As a little bit of reflection reveals, a typical firm’s total profit is zero when price equals average cost (when price equals average cost, total revenue equals total cost). Since we know that total profits are zero at the equilibrium, and we know that the equilibrium price is p′, it must be that the equilibrium firm size is x′ since this is where the firm’s size implies an average cost equal to p′.

This study investigated the influence of median opening length on driving behaviors from a behavioral perspective in the crossover work zone based on a driving simulation study with five different median opening lengths. Four driving performance metrics including speed, acceleration, maximum steering wheel speed, and lane-changing trajectory were selected while analyzing.
The results indicated that there were significant differences of each driving performance metric among various median opening lengths  in the process  of crossing  through  the median  opening  on the entrance  by-pass  and exit by-pass.  Speeding  was a general problem in the crossover work zone because of the speed preference heterogeneity and speed limit compliance differential. The high proportion of speeding vehicles would cause an increase in speed variance, especially when crossing through the median opening with a larger length. In addition, the speed variance would also increase when crossing through a narrower median opening because drivers may sharply decelerate and even decelerate while lane-changing to cross the narrow median successfully. These behaviors would not only induce stronger subjective discomfort but also influence the surrounding vehicles and increase the likelihood of rear-end collisions because the lag vehicle may fail to react with the unexpected headway reduction in time. The improper lane-using behaviors were also observed, especially when crossing the median opening with a large length. It can be explained by the lower mental load, lower risk perception,  and less urgent  lane-changing  demand  caused  by the excessive  lane-changing  space  provided  by the large  median
2. Speed limits in work zones should be used with caution. Variable speed limits are recommended, and their real-time values should be modified by the mean speed and speed variance in crossover work zones. In particular, speed limits in the activity area should be adjusted in accordance with the median opening length to increase the compliance and decrease the speed preference heterogeneity  among  drivers.  In this research,  the combination  of the speed  limit (60 km/h)  and the median  opening  length  (90 m) is recommended on the simulated freeway. 3. Striking temporary markings with removable material are recommended to define temporary lanes on the entrance by-pass and exit by-pass. Signage can also be set in advance to inform drivers to follow the temporary markings when crossing through the median opening. 4. The distances between lane S2 and the channelizing devices are recommended to widen to the median shoulder width, aiming to balance the usage of the opposite lanes and improve the mobility in double-lane designed crossover work zones. In addition, since the traffic space of S3 is narrowed, the temporary usage of the hard shoulder on the opposite roadway should be allowed.
Although  this study  contributes  to investigate  the influence  of the median  opening  length  on driving  behaviors,  there  are still extended works to be finished by future studies. Since the speed preference heterogeneity, the driving performance of the larger sized vehicles,  such as trucks  and buses,  may vary a lot from the standard  passenger  car applied  in this study.  Therefore,  the simulated vehicle types could be enriched to optimize the current study. Based on the findings of the simulation experiments, on-field tests are also needed  to validate  the results  obtained  and investigate  the effects  of the proposed  traffic  management  strategies.  In addition, whether other factors such as gender and age can introduce bias in the driving performance when crossing through the median opening should  be assessed  in future  research.  Finally,  the influence  of other  traffic  control  devices  in other  multi-designed  crossover  work zones on driving behaviors could also be a fruitful area for future work to further improve the safety and mobility in work zones.
Nevertheless, this study includes some limitations. Firstly, the fixed PC-based driving simulator could not produce similar vehicle movements  from the real driving  situation.  Secondly,  some  negative  factors  in the real world,  such as violations  of other  drivers, limited sight distance, and fatigue driving, are not considered in this study. Finally, the absence of the traffic in the opposite direction may also make the simulation experiment different from the real condition.

Thematic analysis revealed nine overarching themes in the data. For the ED groups eight themes emerged: Eating Disorder, which consisted of three sub-themes, Course of Illness (e.g. fear of relapse or inability to recover), Weight and Shape Concerns (e.g. feeling or looking fat, or gaining weight), Behaviors (e.g. engaging in ED behaviors such as vomiting or exercise); Experience of Negative Emotions (e.g. feelings of depression, unhappiness, sadness, uncertainty, suicidality, or having thoughts of death); Rejection & Abandonment (e.g. fear of ending up alone, isolated, or being without friends); Negative Perception of Self (e.g. perceptions of failure, personal inadequacies, or feeling like a bad person);
Interpersonal Relationships, which consisted of two sub-themes, Fear of Negative Evaluation by Others (e.g. fear of negative judgments of others or standing in the way of other people’s lives) and Concerns about close others (e.g. the health or general happiness of family and friends); Lost Opportunities and Regrets (e.g. a lack of achievement, fear of having missed out, or wasted life); Practical Concerns which consisted of two sub-themes, Finance (e.g. not having enough money) and Housing (e.g. having to move or being homeless); and Career Concerns which consisted of two subthemes, Work (e.g. not doing one’s job well or not making progress) and University/College (e.g. not finishing one’s course, not passing exams, or not making career progress).
Table 4 shows the proportion of worries in each of the worry themes, (both initial worry step and penultimate worry steps) for the AN, BN and HC groups separately as well as for the combined ED group (AN þ BN). Generally, the same themes were relevant for the AN and BN groups, and there were only some small differences in terms of proportion of worries in each of the themes (for details please refer to Table 4). Whilst within the ED group some of the initial worries fell into the themes: Practical Concerns (28%), Interpersonal Relationships (11%), and Career Concerns (9%), the majority of worries were ED related (52%). However, although 52% of worries started off as relevant to ED pathology, by the end stages, the themes were as follows e Interpersonal (32%), Negative Perception of Self (22%), Experience of Negative Emotions (20%), Lost Opportunities and Regrets (15%) and Rejection and Abandonment (10%), Eating Disorder (1%).
For the HC participants, almost half the initial worries fell into the Career Concerns theme (49%). HC worries also related to Practical Concerns (19%) and Interpersonal Relationships (18%) themes and to a lesser degree into the Future Options (5%), Experience of Negative Emotions (3%), Eating Disorder (3%) and Negative Perception of Self (3%) themes. For the final worries, the proportions in each theme were as follows: Interpersonal Relationship (29%), Experience of Negative Emotions (23%), Lost Opportunities and Regrets (12%), Rejection and Abandonment (12%), Future options (10%), Negative Perception of Self (6%), Career Concerns (6%), and Practical Concerns (2%).

title: Limasawa: Site of the First Mass

Limasawa: Site of the First Mass
Was it really Limasawa or Butuan? Debates continue on where first Mass was
held here in the Philippines. There is a controversy regarding the site of the first Mass
ever celebrated on Philippine soil. Pigafetta, the Italian chronicler of the Magellan
expedition, tells us that it was held at Easter Sunday, the 31st of March 1521, on an
island called “Mazaua”. Two native chieftains were in attendance; the rajah of Mazaua
and the rajah of Butuan. After the Mass, party went up a little hill and planted a wooden
cross upon its summit. In this case, the subject of the controversy is the identity of
Mazaua. There are two conflicting claims regarding this: one school of thought points to
the small island south of Leyte whereas, the other school rejects that claim and points
instead the beach called “masao”, at the mouth of the Agusan River in northern
Mindanao, near the village (now the city) of Butuan. Judging from the facts presented
and basing from the information and evidences which I have researched, I affirm that
the first mass in the Philippines was held in Limasawa.
The first evidence to support my argument in accordance to the accounts of
Pigafetta and Francisco Albo who are eye-witnesses of the Magellan’s voyage both
stated that the first mass in the Philippines took place on an island called Mazava in
Albo’s account and Mazaua in Pigafetta’s account. They both asserted that from the
island of Homonhon they went westward towards the island of Leyte and turned to a
southwest direction to reach this island. Based on this geographic locations provided by
Albo and Pigafetta, the island of Limasawa in Southern Leyte is the counterpart. On the
contrary, the statement of Father Fernando Colins, a historian, in his work Labor
Evangelica, he asserted that Magellan went to Butuan and there he celebrated the first
Mass and erected a cross. And to support this, Antonio Pigafetta testified that he gave a
gift of certain things to the queen Mother of France — Louise of Savory and mother of
Francis I. Gian Battista Ramusio mentioned that a copy of Pigafetta’s account was
given to Louise of Savory. Whereas, this manuscripts were translated to French by
Jacques Fabre and imprinted by Simon de Colins. And also, there was a monument
erected during 1872 to commemorate the First Mass in Butuan on April 8,1521. In my
opinion, Ramusio’s version of Pigafetta’s manuscripts are not reliable. The transmissions of text from Pigafetta to Louise of Savoy to Simon de Coline is without
documentary support. Pigafetta himself did not mention that he gave a copy of his
manuscript to Louise of Savoy but simply a gift of a certain thing. And I would like to
point out, based on Father Colin’s account, Magellan and his men went to Cebu on
April,1521. But in the monument inscription, the first mass was held on April, 1521 on
Butuan. It is not possible to go back to Butuan from Cebu in just one day on the same
day of the mass wherein, Butuan is 236 kilometers away from Cebu and the ships back
then were not that fast enough. On the same day of the mass, a cross was erected on
the summit of a mountain and according to Francis Albo, at the summit of the mountain,
you can see three islands from west and southwest whereas, Butuan can be seen in the
North direction. Based on the topographical details given by Albo and Pigafetta, it
describes the present Limasawa.
Secondly, Magellan did not go to Butuan to meet the king there. According to
Pigafetta and Albo, while in the island of Mazaua, they met two chieftains: one is the
chieftain of Mazaua and one is the chieftain of Butuan who was said to be visiting the
island. This oppose to the book written Historia de Mindanao y Jolo written by Francisco
Combes S. who worked as a missionary in the Philippines. He stated that Magellan
went to Butuan because they heard the king in Butuan is more powerful that they
wanted to meet him. It was said that their expectations were satisfied by the king. As a
result, they planted a cross on a hill in a solemn ceremony as sign of future alliance. In
Francisco Colin’s Work, the first mass occurred the same day they planted a cross. In
this case, I hereby agree to Pigafettas’s and Albo’s account because they are eye-
witnesses and considered as first-hand accounts. Pigafetta’s work is the most detailed
and reliable source of information regarding Magellan’s voyage compared to the claims
stated by second hand accounts.
Although the evidences presented came from only two accounts, those
evidences are considered as primary sources. The corroboration of information and
statements on those two were present while the Pro-Butuan claims are mostly based
from second hand accounts. Even though their claims are supported by other historians,

title: Critical Friendship
resource:
A key cultural practice of the school is embracing mutual critique regardless of individual staff members’ official positions. The principal, for example, has one of the newly appointed teachers as his critical friend. This was a deliberate move to model that everyone is subject to this critique. Together, the physical geography of the classrooms, teaching practices and the leadership team’s support in fostering critical friendship are essential elements in this cultural critical friendship logic of practice. One leader had earlier blogged about this, saying:
Each critical friend pairing must comment openly on each other’s professional practices. Everyone is a critical friend to someone else in the school: it is both a professional and appraisal edge to ensure that everyone is certain of their responsibilities as teachers; blogging is one outlet to foster it. As one senior leader observed, ‘we all blog to develop a sense of what we do here, to reflect and think on what and how we practise’ (L-Interview, August-2013). One teacher noted that blogging was a:
Another said that, ‘blogging is more about sorting out my thoughts. That process of writing it out ... is an emerging reflection ...’ (S-Interview, May-2014). The same teacher said he was ‘quite happy to discuss the things that are going on in my mind, which means anybody can also critique my teaching’, feeling a ‘responsibility to do it ... [in] improving my own practice’ (S-Interview, May-2014).
Besides blogging, professional e-portfolios help all staff to ‘develop an online portfolio for reflecting on sharing professional learning as well as providing a process for gathering evidence on their teaching’ (C-Blog, 3 February-2014). This combination of online reflections and face-to-face open critique features strongly in the emerging school culture. One teacher said that reflective teaching via blogging or an e-portfolio was about ‘...constantly thinking and conversing about learning’. He also remarked that in the staffroom, ‘people will sit during the lunchtime discussing learning and trying different things, how to support different learning strategies’ (S-Interview, May-2014), and openly sharing different ideas.
Teachers’ open conversations about improving their pedagogical practices demonstrate the developing professional logic of practice centred on critique and reflection. This closely links with the critical friendships, the blogging and the modelling by the senior leaders, building strong staff relationships and an open professional culture. This openness is evidence of both deepening trust and embedding critical friendship into the logic of practice.
Another aspect of this wider view of critical friendship relates to a boy arriving at the school once the school year had started during the second term. This boy’s antagonistic behaviours promoted another student to say (overhead by a staff member and discussed during interviews) something like ‘We don’t behave like that here. You don’t have to do that’. This illustrates how quickly a logic of practice can become embodied by both students and teachers, and in turn adds to the cultural capital of an institution. The actions of this newcomer brought him into sharp relief, as well as demonstrating the rules of engagement in action, as his initial cultural capital did not fit with the prevailing logic. Within three weeks (when we arrived for the data collection), the apparent change in his demeanour and actions had been both positive and remarkable, according to staff.

title: Removing the Mentally Ill from Jails
resource:
The odyssey of repeated incarceration for severely ill people like George Wooten was common in the United States in the early 1800s although many Americans found such practices inhumane and uncivilized. Their sentiments found organized expression in the Boston Prison Discipline Society, which was founded in 1825 by the Reverend Louis Dwight, a Yale graduate and Congregationalist minister. Shocked by what he saw when he began taking Bibles to inmates in jails, he established the society to publicly advocate improved prison and jail conditions in general and hospitals for mentally ill prisoners in particular. According to the medical historian, Gerald Grob, Dwight's "insistence that mentally ill persons belonged in hospitals aroused a responsive chord, especially since his investigations demonstrated that large numbers of such persons were confined in degrading circumstances."3 
Dwight's actions led the Massachusetts legislature to appoint a committee in 1827 to investigate conditions in the state's jails. The committee's report, which was directed to the State General Court, included documentation that many "lunatics and persons furiously mad" were being confined, often in inhumane and degrading conditions. In one jail, a man had been kept for nine years. "He had a wreath of rags around his body and another round his neck. … He had no bed, chair or bench … a heap of filthy straw, like the nest of swine, was in the corner. … The wretched lunatic was indulging [in] some delusive expectations of being soon released from this wretched abode."4

The committee report concluded, "The situation of these wretched beings calls very loudly for some redress. They seem to have been considered as out of the protection of laws. Less attention is paid to their cleanliness and comfort than to the wild beasts in their cages, which are kept for show."5 
Among the specific recommendations of the committee was that all mentally ill inmates of jails and prisons should be transferred to the Massachusetts General Hospital and that confinement of mentally ill persons in the state's jails should be made illegal. Three years later, the Massachusetts General Court "overwhelmingly approved a bill providing for the erection of a state lunatic hospital for 120 patients"; this opened in 1833 as the State Lunatic Asylum at Worcester. When the hospital opened, "more than half of the 164 patients received during that year came from jails, almshouses, and houses of correction [prisons]."6 One-third of these patients had been confined in these institutions for longer than 10 years. 
Dorothea Dix, the most famous and successful psychiatric reformer in American history, picked up where Dwight had left off. In 1841, with the American asylum-building movement under way, Dix began a campaign that would focus national attention on the sad plight of the mentally ill in jails and prisons and would be directly responsible for the opening of at least 30 more state psychiatric hospitals. 

At the time she began her crusade, Dix was a 39-year-old teacher who had been left a bequest by her grandmother, allowing her to give up teaching. Her father had been "shiftless, poverty stricken and irresponsible … fanatically religious, with a penchant for writing theological tracts in fits of 'inspiration,'"7 and her childhood had therefore been very difficult. Her father may in fact have been mentally ill, which would account in part for her zeal to improve conditions for such sufferers. 
Dix's crusade began in early 1841, when she agreed to teach a Sunday school class at the East Cambridge Jail outside Boston. While there, she noticed not only that there were insane prisoners among the inmates, but also that the insane prisoners had no heat in their cells. When she inquired about this, she was told by the jailer that it was because "the insane need no heat." Horrified, Dix reported her findings to her friends and set out to investigate other jails in Massachusetts to ascertain whether similar conditions prevailed. Over the next year, she visited dozens of jails and almshouses and then presented a report to the state legislature. It rang of reform and set the tone for Dorothea Dix's future work: 
After finishing her report in Massachusetts, Dix moved on to New Jersey, where she proceeded in the same fashion to visit jails and almshouses, then report to the state legislature and urge the building of public psychiatric hospitals in which insane persons could be treated humanely and receive treatment. By 1847, she had taken her crusade to many eastern states and visited 300 county jails, 18 prisons, and 500 almshouses. Her success in persuading state legislatures to build psychiatric hospitals was impressive, and she provided a major impetus to the reform movement. 
The Reverend Louis Dwight and Dorothea Dix were remarkably successful in leading the effort to place mentally ill persons in public psychiatric hospitals rather than in jails and almshouses. By 1880, there were 75 public psychiatric hospitals in the United States for the total population of 50 million people. In 1880, the first complete census of "insane persons" in the United States was carried out. It was, in fact, a more complete census than has ever been carried out since and included letters to all physicians asking them to enumerate all "insane persons" in their community, a question about "insanity" on the census form that went to every household, and a canvassing of all hospitals, jails, and almshouses. A total of 91,959 "insane persons" were identified, of which 41,083 were living at home, 40,942 were in "hospitals and asylums for the insane," 9,302 were in almshouses, and only 397 were in jails. The total number of prisoners in all jails and prisons was 58,609, so that severely mentally ill inmates constituted only 0.7 percent of the population of jails and prisons.

While  we  have  detailed  consumers  cancelling  celebrities  and  brands  in  the  consumer cancel  culture  triad,  we  have  not  focused  on  celebrities  cancelling  brands  and  vice-versa. This  is  because  celebrities  can  change  the  companies  they  are  associated  with  in  case  of disagreements  and  similarly,  brands  can  change  their  celebrity  endorsers  regardless  of cancel  culture.  Future  research  could  investigate  these  other  forms  of  cancellation.
Our cancel  culture  framework  was mainly  based  on  power  within  relationships theory. Other  theories  such  as  signaling  and  attribution  could  contribute  to  this  area.  The  most commonly  implemented  application  of  signaling  theory  lies  in  a  firm’s  service  failure  and recovery  communication  efforts.  However,  future  research  could  integrate  signaling theory  in  the  context  of  cancel  culture  to  gauge  how  strong  signals  could  potentially be  less  effective  in  recovering  from  relationship  violations  (Kharouf  et  al.,  2020).  Another avenue of research could consider moral reputation and how its potential interaction with other  factors  including  societal  damage  could  be  examined  in  the  context  of  cancel culture  (Zhou  &  Whitla,  2013).
Additionally,  there  are  five  points  to  note  for  the  future  research  agenda  on  cancel culture.  Firstly,  the  present  paper  does  not  adopt  a  particular  moral  stance  on  this phenomenon  but  explores  it  from  a  consumer-behaviour  perspective.  Future  research could  examine  whether  cancelling  celebrities  and  brands  results  in  positive  outcomes for  these  entities:  whether  cancelling  the  celebrity  or  brand  has  actually  improved their  overall  perception  and  brand  position  in  a  favourable  manner.  This  could  also  be explored  from  a  social  marketing  perspective.  Secondly,  researchers  could  empirically examine  consumers’  perceptions  and  reactions  leading  to  cancellation.  More  interesting  would  be  insights  into  the  particular  roles  that  power  dimensions  play  in  generating  loyalty  and  purchase  interest  as  evidenced  in  extant  research  (Fournier  & Alvarez,  2012).  Popular  cultural  articles  on  cancel  culture  observe  that  cancel  culture does  not  have  lasting  consequences  unless  a  product  or  celebrity  crosses  the  threshold  after  which  a  comeback  is  not  possible.  What  is  the  role  of  warmth  and  competence  in  this  regard?  Empirical  research  could  also  be  centred  around  testing  the valence  of  the  power  dimensions:  whether  increasing  warmth  helps  consumers  to avoid  cancelling  influence  targets;  or  whether  increasing  both  power  dimensions impact  consumers’  overall  cancelling  behaviours.  Thirdly,  research  could  describe the  impact  cancelling  has  on  brands  by  examining  cancel  culture  from  the  company-celebrity  perspective.  For  instance,  what  is  the  effect  on  the  brands  endorsed  by a  cancelled  celebrity  and  vice-versa.  Next,  studies  could  examine  and  extend  the future  research  agenda  in  Merlo  et  al.  (2004)  in  the  context  of  cancel  culture:  for example,  the  underlying  reasons  why  some  customers  are  more  powerful  than  others, whether  because  they  are  interconnected,  or  because  they  are  unsubstitutable. Finally,  the  outcomes  of  cancel  culture  can  be  fine-tuned  and  examined  empirically, such  as  through  study  of  the  loyalty,  cancelled  contracts  and  the  brands’  likelihood  of repositioning.

This randomized, placebo-controlled, crossover study demonstrates that, compared with subjects who consumed alcohol and placebo, subjects who took alcohol and hydrogen had significantly lower BrACs, especially 30 min, 60 min, and 90 min after drinking. The increased efficiency of hydrogen water and hydrogen gas to remove alcohol resulted in reduced hangover symptoms and improved attention and executive functions. The use of hydrogen and sex difference correlated with BrAC and hangover symptoms.
A previous study has demonstrated that ERW inhibits acute ethanol-induced hangovers and decreases the blood alcohol concentration in Sprague-Dawley rats (27). It is known that ERW produced near the cathode during water electrolysis contains a large amount of dissolved molecular hydrogen (28). Based on previous studies, we conducted a human study to further confirm the effects of hydrogen on alcohol metabolism and hangover symptoms. Interestingly, we found different effects of hydrogen on males and females. Hydrogen treatment significantly decreased BrAC in males but not in females. However, hydrogen decreased hangover symptoms not only in males but also in females. The discrepancy could be explained by the following notions. First, after consuming comparable amounts of ethanol, females have higher blood ethanol concentrations than males (29). Second, in males, the increased efficiency of hydrogen to remove alcohol contributes, at least in part, to the relief of hangover symptoms by hydrogen. Third, in females, the decrease in hangover symptoms by hydrogen may depend on other functions of hydrogen, rather than its ability to remove the alcohol. Fourth, low statistical power caused by a small sample size might be one of the reasons.
In females, even if the BrAC was still higher in the hydrogen group, the subjects had substantially reduced hangover symptoms. They experienced fewer headaches, less tiredness, less depression, and less sweating than the normal hangover conditions of the placebo. These symptoms are generally observed during an alcohol hangover (30, 31), and the sum of the scores for all of the questions was significantly lower in the hydrogen group, indicating that hydrogen had a positive, long-term effect rather than a short-term effect on alcohol removal. BrAC and blood alcohol concentration are in direct correlation with each other. Therefore, by measuring BrAC, we are essentially measuring the amount of alcohol in a person’s blood (32). Some studies report a significant correlation between blood alcohol concentration and hangover severity, but the most convincing is the significant relation between immune factors and hangover severity (33). That means the level of alcohol is not a unique factor for hangover symptoms, and we can think about the antioxidant effects of hydrogen. Hydrogen is well known as an antioxidant (12, 34), suggesting that it could help remove liver-harming oxidative substances caused by alcohol consumption (35) and that its antioxidant effects might stimulate alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH) and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase (ALDH) (36), which are most abundant in the liver and are the main enzymes involved in ethanol metabolism in humans. We hypothesize that the antioxidant effects of hydrogen improve alcohol metabolism and relieve hangover symptoms in the long term.
We found that both BrAC and hangover severity were higher in females than in males, and regression analysis showed that female sex was positively associated with BrAC and the survey of hangover symptoms, indicating that sex differences are associated with the presence and severity of alcohol hangover symptoms, which is consistent with several previous reports (37– 39).

Interestingly, we found that systolic BP was decreased after drinking alcohol for 2 h and consumption of hydrogen reversed this decrease (Supplemental Figure 2). A recent meta-analysis confirmed the findings of experimental studies, demonstrating an acute biphasic effect of ethanol on BP, decreasing up to 12 h of ingestion and increasing after 12 h (40). In the present study, consumption of hydrogen reversed the short-term decrease in BP by alcohol. However, we did not observe any change in BP with hydrogen in healthy participants without alcohol consumption (data not shown).
Although we chose a study design robust enough to provide a definitive result for the effect of hydrogen on alcohol consumption and hangover symptoms, we are aware of the study’s limitations. First, we measured BrAC during 3 h without directly measuring blood alcohol concentration, acetaldehyde, ADH, and ALDH activities and genotypes. For better confirmation, it is necessary to measure levels of alcohol, acetaldehyde, ADH, and ALDH until they become undetectable. Second, the small sample size of our study may not be conducive to identifying weak associations because of low statistical power. Low statistical power might be one of the reasons for the discrepancy of the effects of hydrogen on BrAC and hangovers. Third, we used 2 kinds of interventions, hydrogen gas inhalation and hydrogen water drinking. The effect of each intervention mode alone on hangover is worth further exploration.
In conclusion, we confirmed that treatment with hydrogen significantly reduced breath alcohol levels, and improved attention and executive functions after alcohol consumption in the short term, and it relieved a variety of hangover symptoms in the long term. Our results suggest that hydrogen might offer a bit of relief for individuals who are suffering from the effects of alcohol consumption. It needs to be explained that, in a public health view, it seems like a better idea to avoid binge-drinking instead of having to inhale or drink hydrogen gas/water before or during the alcohol intake.

title: DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN PROPTECH
resource:
The real estate sector, traditionally viewed as a brick-and-mortar industry, has been undergoing a significant metamorphosis, driven by the rapid advancements in digital technology. This transformation, often referred to as the digital transformation in PropTech, is reshaping the way properties are bought, sold, and managed, bringing about efficiencies and creating new opportunities.
At the onset of this transformation, the industry witnessed the digitization of property listings and management. The cumbersome paper-based processes started giving way to digital platforms. Property management software, online listing platforms, and digital lease agreements began to emerge, offering convenience and efficiency. These platforms, equipped with advanced algorithms, could match potential buyers with suitable properties, making the property search process more streamlined and personalized.
As the digital wave continued to sweep the industry, the integration of advanced technologies like Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) began to take center stage. These technologies enabled predictive analytics, where property developers could forecast market trends and make informed decisions. For instance, AI-driven tools could predict property price fluctuations, helping investors make timely investment decisions. Additionally, ML algorithms could analyze tenant behavior, assisting property managers in ensuring timely rent collections and property maintenance (Johnson & Johnson, 2017).
The digital transformation in PropTech also saw the integration of blockchain technology, particularly in property transactions. The transparency, security, and efficiency offered by blockchain made it an attractive proposition for the real estate sector. Smart contracts, powered by blockchain, began to replace traditional contracts, ensuring that property transactions were not only faster but also more secure. The decentralized nature of blockchain also reduced the reliance on intermediaries, further streamlining the transaction process (Casino, Dasaklis, & Patsakis, 2019).
In the midst of this digital upheaval, the concept of virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) began to gain traction. These technologies offered immersive property viewing experiences. Potential buyers could take virtual tours of properties, eliminating the need for physical visits. This was particularly beneficial for international property transactions, where buyers could explore properties in different countries without leaving their homes (Alharthi, Alharbi, & Alhindi, 2022).
However, the digital transformation journey in PropTech is not devoid of challenges. The rapid integration of technology also brings with it concerns related to data privacy and security. With vast amounts of data being stored and processed digitally, ensuring that this data is protected from breaches is paramount. Additionally, the industry needs to address the regulatory challenges that come with the adoption of new technologies.
Yet, the potential benefits of the digital transformation in PropTech far outweigh the challenges. The efficiencies brought about by technology, the new revenue streams created, and the enhanced user experiences are testament to the positive impact of this transformation.

In this digital era, from the first online property listing to the advanced AI-driven predictive analytics, the digital transformation in PropTech is not just an evolution; it's a revolution that is setting the stage for the future of the real estate industry.

Whereas other green tea leaves are usually steeped whole in hot water, “matcha is much more concentrated in terms of the ingredients because it’s made from ground whole tea leaves,” said Dr. Frank Hu, a professor of nutrition and epidemiology and chair of the department of nutrition at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health.
Antioxidants. “As we age or as we’re exposed to things in the environment, like ultraviolet light or carcinogens, we end up with reactive oxygen species and they do harmful things like damage our cellular membranes,” said Jamie Alan, an associate professor of pharmacology and toxicology at Michigan State University.

Antioxidants, which are abundant in matcha, are substances that “neutralize” those harmful molecules, Dr. Alan said, preventing a “whole cascade of damaging downstream events.” The tea therefore may theoretically help protect the body’s cells from damage and reduce the risk of certain health problems like heart disease or cancer, Dr. Hu and Dr. Alan said, though this has not been proven.
L-theanine. This unique amino acid, which can be found in green tea as well as certain mushrooms, is another component of matcha that experts highlight as potentially benefiting health. However, the evidence on how it might do so is weak, Dr. Hu said. Some small, placebo-controlled trials have suggested that L-theanine may improve cognitive performance and reduce stress. But there have been only animal studies and a few small trials in humans, both experts noted.
Caffeine. While most people might not think about caffeine’s health effects when drinking their morning cup of coffee, the evidence for its health benefits is fairly strong, Dr. Hu said. Studies have found, for instance, that caffeine can increase cognitive function and alertness and ramp up metabolism. And regular consumption of coffee — the primary source of caffeine for adults in the United States — has been associated with a reduced risk of diabetes, heart disease, liver disease and age-related cognitive decline, Dr. Hu said.

title: Design obligations – the difference

• Where the obligation on the designer is one of reasonable skill and care, negligence has to be proved. • Where there is an obligation of fitness for purpose, which is an unqualified obligation to achieve a result, there is no need to prove negligence as it is irrelevant how carefully the designer has gone about their work. • Is this distinction fair? • It could be said that this approach is reasonable since design and build contracts are usually lump sum or fixed price contracts and a fitness for purpose obligation is a safeguard against the contractor saving costs and maximising profit by carrying out the design to the minimum acceptable standard for buildings of a particular type.
• ‘should a term of reasonable fitness for purpose be implied, or is it that in matters of the design, specification and supervision of the works, (the contractor’s obligation) is .. limited to the exercise of reasonable care and skill. It is worthy of note that they admit an implied obligation, unqualified by negligence, to use materials of good quality and that they also admitted during the hearing the further obligation that those materials should be reasonably fit for the purpose ‘subject to the terms of the contract’. I confess at the outset that I find it difficult to comprehend why an entire contract to build an installation should need to be broken into so many pieces with differing criteria of liability. The virtue of an implied term of fitness for purpose is that it prescribes a relatively simple and certain standard of liability based on the ‘reasonable’ fitness of the finished product, irrespective of considerations of fault and of whether its unfitness derived from the quality of work or materials or design.’ • However, the court again stressed the need for reliance on the skill and judgment of the contractor.
Design obligations – the difference • On the other hand, there is the argument, that construction work is too complex to be equated with the manufacture of a product so what the employer is really ‘buying’ in most cases is the contractor’s design expertise. • This latter view can be seen at first instance in Trebor Bassett Holdings Ltd & Anor v ADT Fire and Security Plc [2012] EWHC 3365 (TCC) where the court rejected an argument that the obligation on a designer and supplier of a bespoke fire suppression system was one of fitness for purpose rather than an obligation to use reasonable skill and care.

• Coulson J said [at 215]:
‘It is worth identifying at the outset the nature of the contract between the parties. It was a contract in which the defendant was to supply to the claimants a system designed to suppress fire in the elevator and/or hopper. That system was made up of various pieces of equipment, such as the sensors and the nozzles, as well as the fire alarm panels and the electrical wiring. But what made it a system (as opposed to a random selection of equipment) was the design: the pulling together of all the relevant information into a designed system that used CO2 to suppress fire in the elevator or hopper. Accordingly, the most important element of the workscope was that done by the defendant's designers: the decision to use a particular piece of equipment in a particular place, with the intention of achieving a particular effect.’
• ‘Another way of expressing the same conclusion is that it is not possible to say of the system supplied that it was in the abstract not of good quality... (W)hat may be a good system for one application may not be a good system for another application. That tends to suggest that the quality of the system cannot be assessed without reference to its intended or actual application...It is a one-off bespoke system, designed for one particular application...(I)t is not a natural or accurate use of language in this context to regard ‘the system’ as simply ‘goods’ attracting without more the well-known statutory incidents of quality and fitness for purpose. What ADT was agreeing to supply was primarily design skills and care in exercising them, not goods, and the goods which they did supply were of good quality.’

title: Introduction
resource:
Within  its  glossary  of  terms,  the  World  Development  Report  2011  (World  Bank  2011) refers to two broad types of justice. One is the larger endeavour of building just and fair societies which  includes  reparative  justice,  restorative  justice,  transformative  justice  and even distributive justice, as potential vehicles to address patterns of exclusion and the lived experiences of injustice. The second, which the World Development Report retreats to as an operational priority in practice, is a justice discourse of institution building. This latter perspective is primarily reliant on service delivery and related (often technocratic) capacity-building approaches, as the confidence-building machinery of the rule of law. These two broad notions of justice are neither necessarily compatible nor entirely separable from each other, but may easily prompt very different approaches, giving rise to different programmatic priorities and responses, with the potential for a significant gap between local programming and global policy interventions—particularly at the intersection between justice and human rights aspirations on one hand, and building sustainable peace on the other. This dilemma is also reflected in the creative tension between the operational imperatives and the policy visions within many peacebuilding as well as human rights organizations.
In addition, the issue of human rights in the prevention of violent conflict and peacebuilding is sometimes still controversial or divisive, especially when associated with criminal justice demands in the context of delicate political negotiations. This article aims to help organizations resolve and optimize this creative tension in carving out a distinctive role  for  peacebuilding  organizations  in  a  justice-based  approach  to  preventing  violent conflict. The arguments that follow challenge the peacebuilding field to engage more proactively and explicitly with human rights and justice, and to embrace a rights and justice-based approach as a core component of conflict prevention, rather than viewing this as a potential  hindrance  to  negotiated  peace  processes  or  delicate  reconciliation  endeavours. The article also challenges the predominantly narrow conceptions of justice, in order to expand the role of justice and human rights in peacebuilding and the prevention of violent conflict. A core intention of the article is therefore to support the development of a collaborative space at the intersection between the human rights and peacebuilding fields. It seeks an innovative and strategic approach to justice and human rights within the peacebuilding sector, and endeavours to offer human rights advocates and actors an alternative framework for the use of justice tools preventively rather than merely retroactively, to pursue long-term peace in conflict-affected and post-conflict societies.
It is important to acknowledge that this article seeks to articulate a strategic approach and an alternative framework for ‘justice as prevention’ that may have vital implications for practical programming and potential for operational innovation. However, constraints of space and focus do not permit a more detailed examination of these operational or programming opportunities for peacebuilding or human rights practitioners. It is important to note, however, that this approach is premised on a diversified understanding of prevention in relation to the instigation, continuation, escalation, recurrence and even transmutation of violent conflict—a peace and conflict continuum. This is distinct from narrower perspectives of post-conflict prevention, and unconstrained by the sometimes unhelpful distinctions in the field between peacemaking, peacekeeping, and peacebuilding as distinct operational phases.
In articulating this framework for the transformative potential of justice as prevention, I draw upon my own personal experience of nearly 30 years as a practitioner, a research scholar, and a policy advocate. I have played these roles in the peacebuilding, human rights, and transitional justice fields, as well as in the fields of criminal justice and security sector reform,  and  through  my  work  on  violence  prevention  and  reconciliation  approaches  in conflict-affected societies. I have supplemented this experiential learning and reflection by undertaking additional desk research, as well as interviews with peacebuilding and justice or  human  rights  practitioners  in  the  field.  Much  of  this  work  and  experience  has  been undertaken  within  national  and  international  civil  society  organizations,  and  in  tandem with social movements and victims’ organizations. However, it has also always been at the interface between these sectors and governmental and multilateral or international organizations. This is particularly important to the analysis of the prevailing practices and challenges for the peacebuilding and human rights sectors that appear below. These dilemmas do not exclusively afflict professional and community-based or civil society organizations, but are equally significant in the policy and practice of national governments, and of peacebuilding,  mediation  and  human  rights  agencies  within  the  multilateral  system  and  the United Nations, as well as in the approaches of many donor agencies. In contemplating the composition of the peacebuilding sector in the pages below, it is important to factor in this full range of divergent actors.
This  article  begins  by  describing  and  challenging  the  notion  of  a  peace  and  justice dichotomy, or the assumption that peace and justice processes are all but incompatible in conflict-affected societies. Then it will set out a three-pronged critique of this orthodoxy and frame an alternative way of thinking about a mutually beneficial ‘peacebuilding and justice continuum’. Thereafter, the article will map current thematic trends within the justice and human rights sector, as well as the gaps and opportunities that these present. The article will conclude with some reflections on justice as rules, institutions and structures, relationships and processes. Throughout, it will assert the need to shift perspective—from justice as a set of normative parameters to justice as a transformative influence in the processes of conflict transformation and peacebuilding.

resource:
A key theoretical contribution of this article is that it addressed the importance of the employee autonomy–work outcome relationship and assessed whether these were always equally strong or weak or contingent on certain boundary factors and conditions. Given the assumption that employees are seeking congruence with their environments [27, 131, 132] and that the work context is undergoing rapid and frequent change [5], the results can help practitioners and researchers better understand the interrelationships between work design features and the broader organizational context.
Therefore, an analysis of the supporting and inhibitive factors in autonomy relationships indicates how organizations can adjust strategies for certain situations and effectively fine-tune work design principles and boundary conditions. Because extant work design theory and research has mostly neglected context contingent perspectives [27], this study saw autonomy as one of the most salient work design features and selected dimensions of the psychological climate as the contingency factors. The results of this study, however, confirmed the results of previous studies that have largely treated autonomy relationships in isolation independent of its moderating potential [35]. Autonomy has a significant impact on employee attitudes and work outcomes (perceived IWB) but the relationship appears to be independent from contextual boundary conditions. Contrary to expectations, the results of this study indicated that organizations do not need to consider the organizational context when putting together work design strategies. Similar findings were found in a study that investigated dispersed collaboration in the front-end of innovation. Specifically, the researchers have tested the moderating influence of the role of communities, as well as organizational climate on the relationship between the proficiency of dispersed collaboration and front-end innovation performance. While climate showed as well a significant direct effect on front-end innovation performance, the researchers also did not find any support for the moderating role of organizational climate in this relationship [133].
The potential reasons for these results, however, should be carefully considered in further evaluations. First, as this study only examined three selected climate dimensions, only a small part of the overall organizational context and the available climate dimensions in the affective, cognitive, and instrumental categories [28] were examined. Further, only a single work design feature within the task characteristics category (autonomy) was examined; therefore, it is likely that when the scope is broadened to include additional work design features such as task variety, feedback, job complexity or social support [35] as well as different climate dimensions [77], the results may be substantially different.
Second, one of the major underlying assumptions of this study was that employees were seeking individual correspondence with their broader work environments [132] through their work behavior, and that correspondence or, “a relationship in which the individual and the environment are corresponsive or mutually responsive” [134], supported or weakened certain relationships. Specifically, climate acts as a cross-level moderator and “shapes the relationship between work characteristics and the consequences of work design” [27]. In this study, however, this did not seem to be the case. A potential reason for this outcome might be that autonomy or its sub-dimensions do not play a role in connection with the selected climate factors. While logical theoretical connections between the autonomy–IWB relationship and the selected context dimensions that were likely to act as cross-level moderators were drawn, it seems that such congruence did not apply to the selected variables. For example, strong supervisor support was expected to positively influence the autonomy–IWB relationship through the inherent discretionary atmosphere and trust in good leader-member cooperation on which an autonomous work design can be built; however, there was no or not a strong enough connection between the climate factor and the work design attribute to trigger a cross-level interaction effect.
Moreover, a second contribution of this article is the consideration of employee autonomy as a multi-faceted construct. The results of the study clearly show that different dimensions of the construct have different results and thus clearly indicate that autonomy should not be considered as a unidimensional construct. This is insofar important, as autonomy has been one of the most salient work design features and has recently (re-)gained enhanced importance due to an increase of knowledge-based organizations in which enhanced employee autonomy has been found to be an important predictor of innovation performance [13, 26]. It is therefore important that future studies analyzing work design relationships including autonomy as a feature consider the multi-faceted nature of autonomy. In retrospective, it would therefore also be interesting to investigate which types of autonomy have been considered in previous studies and how the results would change when using other dimensions of autonomy (e.g., work methods autonomy or decision-making autonomy instead of work scheduling autonomy which has been used predominantly).
